sentences.text: Amygdalodon is an extinct genus of basal sauropod known for its almond-shaped teeth.
The name refers to laterally compressed teeth that were slightly curved inward.
These teeth were spatulate in shape and lacked denticles on their crowns.
Amygdalodon is one of the few Jurassic dinosaurs known from South America.
It represents the only evidence in South America for a probable early Middle Jurassic basal eusauropod, suggesting global dispersal.
The holotype, discovered in 1936, includes vertebrae, ribs, teeth, a partial pelvis, and a shoulder blade.
The type species Amygdalodon patagonicus was described by Cabrera in Argentina in 1947.
The fossils were donated to the Museo de La Plata and cataloged as number 46-VIII-21-1.

Derived dental characters in Amygdalodon, such as crown-to-crown occlusion and buccal and lingual grooves, suggest some traits previously thought unique to Eusauropoda appeared earlier in sauropod evolution.
Rauhut (2003) classified Amygdalodon as Eusauropoda incertae sedis based on the type material.
A cladistic analysis by Carballido et al. (2010) recovered Amygdalodon as a non-eusauropod sauropod.
Holwerda and Pol (2018) recovered Amygdalodon as the sister taxon to Isanosaurus.
Pol and colleagues (2022) supported a basal sauropod classification for Amygdalodon, noting early signs of dental modification for bulk feeding but lacking derived vertebral features.
Amygdalodon is considered a Cetiosauridae due to specific vertebral features with only simple lateral depressions.
Based on phylogenetic analysis, Amygdalodon is interpreted as a non-eusauropod sauropod.
Due to the fragmentary nature of the available material, alternative positions placing Amygdalodon within Eusauropoda exist.
Fossils of Amygdalodon have been found in the Toarcian-aged Cerro Carnerero Formation, dating to about 180-172 million years ago.
Amygdalodon lived during the Middle Jurassic, approximately 180 to 171 million years ago, in what is now Argentina.
Remains of Amygdalodon were found in Chubut Province, east of the Sierra de Pampa de Agnía locality in Patagonia, Argentina.
It is debated whether the material represents very basal non-neosauropod eusauropods.
